theory.intro: When a finite derivative exists, the **instantaneous rate of change** of $f(x)$ at $x = a$ is the rate at that single moment. It is the gradient of the **tangent** to the curve at $(a, f(a))$, written $f'(a)$.
facts: The instantaneous rate of change at $x = a$ is written $f'(a)$, read "$f$ prime of $a$".
When a finite derivative exists at $a$, the secant gradient approaches the tangent gradient as the second point approaches $(a,f(a))$.
A tangent sloping upwards means the instantaneous rate is positive, $f'(a) > 0$.
A horizontal tangent means $f'(a) = 0$, which is a stationary point.
A tangent sloping downwards means the instantaneous rate is negative, $f'(a) < 0$.
steps: Identify the point of interest $(a, f(a))$ on the curve.
Recognise that the instantaneous rate is the gradient of the tangent line at that single point.
Read two convenient points on the tangent and calculate its gradient: rise divided by run, $\dfrac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}$. Use the labelled axis scales.
Interpret the value of $f'(a)$ in context with appropriate rate units.

foundation.question_text:
A cup of coffee cools on a desk.
The temperature graph is steep at first and becomes flatter as it approaches room temperature.
Explain what is happening to the instantaneous rate of cooling over time.
foundation.solution_text:
$\text{The tangent line to the temperature curve becomes less steep (closer to horizontal) as time passes.}$
$\text{This means the instantaneous rate of cooling decreases in magnitude over time as the temperature nears room temperature.}$
